title: Silencing the Span
summary: An open research programme that defines the subway rail-noise problem from the Manhattan Bridge in DUMBO, Brooklyn, as the evidence a design-build intervention would need before procurement.

narrative.problem: B, D, N and Q trains cross the Manhattan Bridge roughly every 76 seconds, about 20 hours a day, and the MTA measured 87.50 dB(A) Leq at the Brooklyn Bridge Park dog run. Twenty-one years of measurement have produced no mitigation: the state rapid-transit noise code leaves the level for elevated structures "to be established", and NYC 311 has no category for rail noise.
narrative.decision: It is deliberately a problem definition, not a design: every citation carries a verification state, each document gets an adversarial red-team pass, and withdrawn claims are quoted in place rather than quietly deleted.
narrative.tradeoff: No option in any document is recommended for procurement, and most findings stay hedged until methods that need records requests, field measurement or surveys are actually carried out.
narrative.limitation: No calibrated acoustic measurement has been taken and no survey has been made; of the 48 methods specified, six have been executed and one partially. None of the documents is peer-reviewed.
narrative.caveat: The acoustic demonstration uses an assumed spectrum, the agent model uses invented itineraries, and the 3D wireframe is inferred geometry rather than a survey.
